lines: In one hundred forty-six B C, one of the richest cities in the Mediterranean burned for days.
Its people were sold as slaves. Its name became a warning.
But here is the strange part. Rome had already beaten this city, fifty years earlier.
And since then, Carthage had paid, obeyed, and asked Rome's permission for almost everything.
So why did Rome come back to finish it?
To answer that, we need a fresh fig, a king who was almost ninety, and one impossible order.
This is how Rome destroyed Carthage, and where you can still walk through what is left of it today.
First, where are we? Carthage stood on the coast of North Africa, right next to Tunis, the capital of Tunisia today.
By tradition, it was founded around eight hundred fourteen B C by sailors from Tyre, a city in today's Lebanon.
For centuries, Carthage lived from the sea.
Its most famous harbour was a perfect circle, with a small island in the middle.
Appian, an ancient historian, says it had sheds for two hundred twenty warships.
Across the sea was Rome. Not an empire yet, but a republic, run by a Senate of powerful families and two consuls elected every year.
The two cities fought two huge wars. In our last video, Hannibal crossed the Alps and nearly broke Rome.
But in two hundred two B C, he lost at Zama.
The peace treaty a year later was harsh. Carthage lost everything outside Africa and kept only a handful of warships.
It had to pay ten thousand talents of silver over fifty years. A talent was about twenty-six kilograms, so that is roughly two hundred sixty tonnes.
And one more rule: Carthage could not fight any war without Rome's permission.
It sounds like a small detail. It will decide everything.
Then Carthage did something nobody expected. It got rich again.
Trade came back, the city grew, and its farms were some of the best in the Mediterranean.
In one hundred ninety-one B C, Carthage even offered to pay the whole debt at once.
Rome said no. A Carthage still paying was a Carthage still on a leash.
So, Carthage lost the war, but it won the peace. And in Rome, some people found that frightening.
One of those people was Marcus Porcius Cato, a tough old senator, famous for hating luxury, and for never changing his mind.
Around one hundred fifty-three B C, Cato visited Carthage. He expected a beaten city.
He found full markets, busy harbours, and a growing population.
Back in Rome, the story goes, he dropped a fresh fig in front of the Senate.
This fig, he said, grew only three days' sail from here.
The message was simple. The enemy is close, and getting stronger.
From then on, ancient writers say, Cato ended every speech, on any subject, with the same words: Carthage must be destroyed.
Not everyone agreed. Another senator, Scipio Nasica, said the opposite: Carthage must be spared.
A dangerous rival, he argued, kept Rome disciplined.
Historians today think the fig story was polished over the centuries. But the fear behind it was very real.
So, Rome's most stubborn senator wanted Carthage gone. All he needed now was an excuse.
The excuse came from next door. West of Carthage lay Numidia, a kingdom covering much of today's Algeria and western Tunisia.
Its king, Masinissa, was Rome's loyal ally. He had fought for Rome at Zama, and Rome let him do almost anything.
For decades, he took bites out of Carthage's land. First the rich coast in the south. Then a whole region of about fifty towns.
Every time, Carthage complained to Rome. Every time, Roman envoys came, looked around, and sided with Masinissa.
Remember the treaty? No war without Rome's permission. So Carthage could only watch.
In one hundred fifty B C, Masinissa besieged another Carthaginian town. This time, Carthage snapped.
It raised an army of about twenty-five thousand men, and marched.
Masinissa was about eighty-eight years old. He still won. Trapped and starving, most of that army never came home.
And watching that battle, by pure chance, was a young Roman officer named Scipio Aemilianus. Remember that name.
So, Carthage had fought a war without asking. In Rome's eyes, it had just broken the treaty.
Rome declared war in one hundred forty-nine B C. Even Utica, Carthage's big neighbour up the coast, switched to Rome's side.
A huge Roman army, about eighty thousand men by one ancient count, gathered in Sicily, a short sail from Carthage.
Carthage tried everything to avoid a war it knew it could not win.
First, Rome asked for hostages: three hundred children from its noblest families. Carthage sent them.
Then the Roman army landed in Africa anyway. Next order: hand over all your weapons. Carthage did.
According to Appian, Roman officers collected armour for two hundred thousand men, and two thousand catapults.
Now Carthage was a rich city with no army, no fleet, and no weapons. Then the consul Censorinus gave the final order.
Leave your city. Rebuild it at least ten miles inland, about fifteen kilometres from the sea. Carthage itself will be torn down.
For a city that lived from fishing, trade, and harbours, this was a death sentence. Just a slower one.
So, Carthage gave up its children and its weapons. Then Rome asked for the city itself. And Carthage said no.
With almost nothing left, Carthage rearmed. People worked day and night, making swords, spears, and catapult bolts.
The story goes that women even cut off their hair, to twist into ropes for the new catapults.
And at first, it worked. Massive walls blocked the land side of the city, and the Roman attacks of the first two years failed.
During the siege, old Masinissa died, at around ninety. Rome's ally was gone, but the war went on.
When the Romans blocked the harbour entrance, Carthage secretly dug a brand-new channel to the sea,
and sailed out a fleet of about fifty warships it had built in hiding.
Rome changed commanders. In one hundred forty-seven B C, the man in charge became Scipio Aemilianus, the young officer who had watched Masinissa's battle.
He sealed the city off by land and by sea. Hunger did the rest.
In the spring of one hundred forty-six B C, the Romans broke into the harbour, then fought street by street for six days and nights.
On the citadel hill, called the Byrsa, the last defenders gave up. About fifty thousand men and women walked out, and were sold into slavery.
Scipio ordered the city burned. And then his friend, the historian Polybius, saw something unexpected. Scipio was crying.
He quoted Homer's lines about the fall of Troy, and said he feared that one day, the same would happen to Rome.
So, after three years of siege, Carthage fell. More than six hundred years of history ended in a few days.
You may have heard that the Romans then plowed the ruins and covered the ground with salt, so nothing would ever grow there again.
It is a great story. But no ancient writer tells it. Not Polybius, who was there. Not Appian. Nobody.
Historians traced the salt story to modern history books, from the early twentieth century. It probably got mixed up with salt curses in other ancient stories.
What Rome really did is simpler. Carthage's land became a Roman province, called Africa, and Scipio cursed anyone who would rebuild the city.
So, the city burned and the land became Roman. But the salt is a modern myth.
The curse did not last. About a hundred years later, Julius Caesar planned a new Roman city on the very same spot, and Augustus built it.
Roman Carthage became one of the great cities of the Roman world. The place Rome tried to erase came back, as Rome.
Today, the ruins lie in a quiet suburb of Tunis, beside the sea, between houses and gardens.
Since nineteen seventy-nine, they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
You can stand on the Byrsa hill where the last defenders surrendered, and look down at the round harbour that once hid a fleet.
Carthage paid its debt, obeyed the treaty, and handed over its weapons. It still was not enough.
For Rome, the problem was never what Carthage did. It was that Carthage existed.
So, was Cato right, and Rome was only safe once Carthage was gone?
Or was Scipio Nasica right, that Rome lost something when it lost its rival? Tell me what you think in the comments.
